1191.title: Guru Amar Das close
1191.hook: humility, equality, and a kitchen open to all
1191.howItsDone: Gurdwaras run a langar, a free kitchen where volunteers cook and serve and everyone sits together on the floor or at shared tables; Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das's part in it, along with his hymns, on his gurpurab.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns of the mind: O restless mind, no one finds Him through cleverness. Your line was rest in the word.

Steam rising off big pots. Someone stirring dal with a paddle as long as an arm. Rows of people on the floor, shoulder to shoulder, and a volunteer coming down the line with a bucket of rotis, one into each open palm. A farmer, a banker, a stranger who wandered in: same floor, same food, same hands serving it. That kitchen is where our time with Guru Amar Das ends, because the hymns of the past days show up in it, cooked down to something you can eat.
screen: `STEAM, DAL, A LONG PADDLE.` → `SAME FLOOR, SAME FOOD.` → `THE HYMNS, COOKED DOWN.`

segments.voice: Three threads run through his time, and the kitchen ties them together. Humility. Tradition remembers him as a servant long before anyone called him Guru, carrying water in the dark. His hymns warn about haumai, ego, and say ego and the Name can't share one room. In the langar, nobody eats in a place of honor. Equality. Tradition remembers his well at Goindval as open to every caste, his teachers on their manjis as women and men, and his voice against a tax on pilgrims. He took the word sati off the pyre and gave it to faithful lives. In the langar, nobody asks who your family is before the roti is handed over. And a kitchen open to all. Sikh tradition gives Guru Amar Das a large part in making the langar central, so that those who came to see the Guru sat in the row and ate first. The meal became a teaching about who belongs. You can hear the old Guru's voice in the clatter of the pots. O mind, you are the form of light, and so, in the Sikh view, is the person beside you. The world is burning, so feed whoever comes, by any door. Face the Guru, not only yourself. Let ego die a little in the serving. And when the mind is restless, rest in the Word, then pick up the bucket and walk the row. Tomorrow, his successor, Guru Ram Das, and the shape of a Sikh's morning.
screen: `HUMILITY: THE WATER CARRIER.` · `EQUALITY: THE WELL, THE MANJIS, THE PYRE.` · `THE ROW BEFORE THE AUDIENCE.` · `THE HYMNS IN THE CLATTER OF POTS.` · then, large: `OPEN KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Picture your own kitchen, your table, or just your free hour this week, and the door to it: who usually comes through, and who never does? Let one person come to mind who could use a seat, a neighbor, a new coworker, someone alone, and see them sitting down as something simple is handed to them. No grand plan, just the door opening.
Guru Amar Das close. Humility, equality and a kitchen open to all: the old Guru's hymns of ego, light and the Word, cooked down into a shared meal. Today's word.
Your line: open kitchen. Nobody is tested at the door before the roti comes. Same time tomorrow.

1192.title: The routine of a Gursikh
1192.hook: Guru Ram Das's salok on the Guru's Sikh: up early, bathed, remembering the Name (Gauri Var M4, ang 305)
1192.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the daily discipline rise in the early hours, bathe, and recite the morning prayers, beginning with the Japji; this salok of Guru Ram Das is one of the passages Sikh teachers turn to when they describe the Sikh day.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Guru Amar Das: humility, equality, and a kitchen where anyone could sit and eat. Your line was open kitchen.

Whoever calls himself a Sikh of the Guru. That's how a short salok begins, in Guru Ram Das's ballad in Raga Gauri. Notice the opening. Not whoever was born into a Sikh family. Not whoever knows the hymns by heart. Whoever claims the name. And instead of a definition, the salok hands you a clock: what that claim looks like before the sun is up. A new voice on the path, Guru Ram Das, whose hymns carry the heading Mahala four. The first thing we hear from him is a morning.
screen: `WHOEVER CALLS HIMSELF A SIKH.` → `NOT A DEFINITION, A CLOCK.` → `MAHALA FOUR.`

segments.voice: The first half of the salok, paraphrased: the one who calls himself a Sikh of the Guru rises in the early hours and dwells on the Lord's Name. He makes the effort, early in the morning, bathes, and dips in the pool of nectar. Following the Guru's teaching, he repeats the Name, and his faults and wrongs fall away. Three things stand out. First, a name turns into a habit. The salok doesn't argue about who counts as a Sikh. It describes a morning and lets the morning answer. Second, the word for effort, udam. Rising early isn't a personality type for the lucky few who wake up cheerful. It's something you make the effort to do, the way a farmer gets up to water a field. Third, the pool of nectar. Some readers hear a real bath, the body washed before the day. Others hear the pool as the Name itself, where the mind gets washed. Some teachers hold both together. Sikhs call those early hours amrit vela, the ambrosial time, a phrase from Guru Nanak's Japji. The salok itself doesn't name the sangat, but for Sikhs near a gurdwara, the morning can mean walking in to hear the prayers with others. So the routine of a Gursikh isn't a rulebook. It's a person whose day starts with remembering, on purpose, before anything else gets a vote.
screen: `A NAME TURNS INTO A HABIT.` · `UDAM: THE EFFORT TO RISE.` · `THE POOL OF NECTAR, BODY AND MIND.` · `BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE GETS A VOTE.` · then, large: `THE ROUTINE OF A GURSIKH.`

segments.voice: Imagine tomorrow's first minutes at a time a little earlier than usual, not heroic, just a little. Choose what the first thing will be, washing your face slowly, a line of Gurbani, a few quiet breaths before the phone, and hold that picture until it feels doable. If you pray, let Waheguru be the first word in it.
The routine of a Gursikh. Guru Ram Das's salok: rise early, make the effort, bathe, and dwell on the Name before the day begins. Today's word.

1193.title: After the morning
1193.hook: then, as the day rises, the Sikh sings the Guru's word and remembers, sitting and standing (Gauri Var M4, ang 305)
1193.howItsDone: Sikh teaching joins remembering the Name with honest work, kirat karni; Sikhs who keep it repeat Waheguru or hum a line of Gurbani through the working day rather than setting the day apart from prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first half of Guru Ram Das's salok: up early, washed, remembering the Name. Your line was the gursikh's morning.

The prayers are finished. The tea is gone. Someone can't find a shoe, the inbox has filled up overnight, and the bus is already at the corner. A quiet morning can last about as long as it takes to open the front door. After that, the day takes over, and by lunch the early hours can feel like they happened to somebody else. Guru Ram Das's salok doesn't end at sunrise. Its second half begins with a small, important word: then.
screen: `THE PRAYERS ARE FINISHED.` → `THE DAY TAKES OVER.` → `THE SALOK SAYS: THEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the second half, paraphrased. Then, as the day rises, he sings the Guru's word. Sitting and standing, he dwells on the Name. The one who remembers the Lord with every breath and every bite, that Gursikh is pleasing to the Guru's mind. Start with then. The morning is a beginning, not the whole of it: the place where remembering gets lit, like a fire, not where it gets finished and put away. Next, sitting and standing. That's the posture of a whole day: at a desk, behind a counter, in a car, on your feet in a kitchen. Some readers hear in it the Sikh teaching of honest work, kirat karni: the Sikh isn't asked to leave the job to remember, but to remember inside it. Then the measure: saas giraas, breath and mouthful, the smallest units a day has. Breaths and bites just keep happening, all day long. So remembering here isn't a block of time you schedule. It's a thread through the things you do anyway. And notice who the salok says is pleased. Not the boss, not the neighbors, not someone keeping score of who prayed longest. The Guru's mind. That quietly changes what a good working day is: not only what got done, but whether the Name came along while it got done.
screen: `THE MORNING IS WHERE IT STARTS.` · `SITTING AND STANDING, AT WORK.` · `SAAS GIRAAS: BREATH AND MOUTHFUL.` · `PLEASING TO THE GURU'S MIND.` · then, large: `AFTER THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: Run through your working day in your mind, where you sit, where you stand, what you eat, and choose one thing that happens again and again, sitting down, a sip of water, a door, as your cue. Each time it comes, one slower breath can remember, silently, with Waheguru if you pray.
After the morning. The second half of the salok: then sing the Guru's word, and sitting and standing, with breath and mouthful, keep the Name close. Today's word.
Your line: work, remembering. The Name can come along while the hands keep working. Rest well.

1194.title: Blessing others
1194.hook: the Guru asks for the dust of the feet of the Sikh who remembers and helps others remember (Gauri Var M4, ang 306)
1194.howItsDone: Sikhs meet this salok when Gauri ki Var is sung or read, and it is quoted when Sikhs speak of the Gursikh's day; looking after shoes at the gurdwara door is one of the forms of seva Sikhs volunteer for.

segments.voice: Yesterday, after the morning: sitting and standing, with breath and mouthful, the Name comes along to work. Your line was work, remembering.

Shoes come off at the door of a gurdwara. In some gurdwaras, volunteers take them, line them up, even wipe the dust off, and the person doing it might be a shopkeeper, a student, or someone with a great deal of money. Dust from other people's feet, handled as an honor. Hold that picture, because Guru Ram Das ends his salok about the Gursikh's day with dust. And the surprise is who's asking for it.
screen: `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `DUST, HANDLED AS AN HONOR.` → `WHO'S ASKING FOR IT?`

segments.voice: The closing lines, paraphrased. The one on whom my Lord is kind, to that Gursikh the Guru gives the teaching. Servant Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of that Gursikh who repeats the Name himself, and leads others to repeat it. Read it slowly; it turns things upside down. The voice is the Guru's, signing with the name Nanak, as the Gurus do in the Granth, and calling himself servant. And the Guru is the one asking, for the dust of a disciple's feet. Touching someone's feet is a gesture of deep respect in Punjab. Asking for the dust from them goes lower still. Next, notice which Sikh he honors this way. The earlier lines already called the Sikh who rises early and remembers through the working day pleasing to the Guru's mind. But the one whose dust the Guru asks for remembers and then helps someone else remember. The salok has been walking outward all along: one person waking, a day of work, other people. And the first line says the teaching comes as kindness. The Gursikh doesn't earn it like a wage. The Lord is kind, and the Guru shares the teaching. So helping someone remember isn't a lecture or a recruiting drive. It's passing on a kindness you were given: a reminder on a hard day, a line of a hymn sent to a friend, an invitation to sit together.

Your line: help others remember. A kindness you were given is meant to travel. Until tomorrow.

1195.title: Wedding horse songs
1195.hook: Guru Ram Das pictures the body as a horse the Lord made, ridden home to the Beloved (Vadhans M4, ang 575)
1195.howItsDone: Guru Ram Das's Ghorian are sung in kirtan in Raga Vadhans, and Sikh teachers read them as a picture of the human body as a gift for the soul's journey to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday finished Guru Ram Das's salok on the Gursikh: the Guru asks for the dust of the feet of the one who helps others remember. Your line was help others remember.

A drum, a crowd in bright clothes, and a groom climbing onto a decorated horse while the women of his family sing. In Punjabi wedding tradition, the songs sung around the groom and his horse have a name: ghorian, horse songs. Family songs, teasing and proud, the kind aunts know by heart. Guru Ram Das took that wedding song and wrote his own, in Raga Vadhans. Same horse, same joy, same ride to the bride's door. But the rider, the road, and the one waiting at the end all change.
screen: `A GROOM ON A DECORATED HORSE.` → `GHORIAN: THE HORSE SONGS.` → `THE GURU WRITES HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's how his Ghorian open, paraphrased. The body is a horse, fashioned by the Lord. Blessed is this human life, received by good fortune. And: this body is the horse on which the Lord is reached. Meeting the True Guru, songs of joy are sung. Four things happen in those lines. First, the borrowing. He doesn't invent a new form. He takes a song people already sing at weddings and lets it carry the Name. Second, the horse is the body. Not a prison, not an enemy to beat into line. A horse the Lord made, a gift received by good fortune. A body is how you get anywhere. Third, the ride. At a wedding, the groom rides to the bride. In the hymn, the ride is the soul going home to the Beloved, the Lord. A whole human life becomes the wedding procession, and the body is the horse that carries it there. Fourth, the songs of joy, sung on meeting the True Guru. The ride isn't a grim march. It has music in it, the way a baraat, the groom's wedding procession, does. And the picture is gentle. A rider who hates the horse doesn't get far. A rider who knows the horse is a gift, feeds it, rests it, and points it the right way, gets to the wedding.

1196.title: Longing for sight
1196.hook: Guru Ram Das's hymns long for the sight of the Beloved and the True Guru (Sri Rag M4, ang 40)
1196.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of going for darsan of the Guru Granth Sahib at the gurdwara and of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, and Guru Ram Das's hymns of longing are sung in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ghorian, Guru Ram Das's wedding horse songs: the body a horse the Lord made, the soul riding home. Your line was ride to the beloved.

What does missing someone actually want? Not news. You can know everything about a person far away, what they ate, where they went, how the weather is, and the ache stays exactly where it was. What it wants is to see them. The face. The door opening, and there they are. Earlier on this path we heard young Arjan's letters home, longing to see his father. Now we hear the father. Guru Ram Das has hymns full of that same ache, and the word at the center of them is sight.
screen: `NOT NEWS. THE FACE.` → `ARJAN'S LETTERS, LONGING.` → `NOW THE FATHER'S VOICE.`

segments.voice: One, from Sri Rag, paraphrased. In my mind and body, the pain of separation is great. How will my Beloved come home and meet me? When I see my Lord, seeing him, the pain goes away. I go and ask my friends: how can I meet the Lord? And the refrain: O my True Guru, without you I have no other. Four things are in there. First, the word for that pain, birha, the ache of being apart from someone you love. The hymn doesn't hide it or hurry past it. It's great, and it's in the mind and the body both. Second, the cure. Not a better argument. Seeing. Sikhs call that seeing darsan: a glimpse of the beloved, of the Guru, of the Lord. Third, the friends. Longing doesn't sit alone at home. It goes out and asks the people who have met the Beloved how they did it. That's one picture of what the sangat is for. Fourth, the refrain turns to the Guru: without you, I have no other. The longing for God and for the Guru run through the same hymn, because in Sikh teaching it's the Guru who shows the way to that sight. And the hymn trusts the longing. It's not a problem to get over. The ache is part of the road. It's what sends you out the door, asking.

1197.title: The city he built
1197.hook: a pool, a bazaar and a sangat: tradition says Guru Ram Das built a place for ordinary life to be holy
1197.howItsDone: Pilgrims to the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar walk through the old bazaars around it on their way in and out, and Sikhs remember Guru Ram Das as the Guru who began the city.

segments.voice: Yesterday, longing for sight: the ache of separation in Guru Ram Das's hymn, and darsan, the seeing that heals it. Your line was longing for sight.

Step out of the gate of the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, and you're not in a quiet garden. You're in the street. Shops, carts, the smell of frying, someone selling bangles, someone haggling over cloth. The Guru's house and a busy market sit side by side, and the crowd doesn't seem to find that strange. Sikh tradition says it was planned that way, from the start, by the Guru who began the city.
screen: `OUT OF THE GATE, INTO THE STREET.` → `HOLY PLACE, BUSY MARKET.` → `PLANNED THAT WAY, TRADITION SAYS.`

segments.voice: Earlier on this path we heard about the pool itself, the pool of nectar at Amritsar. Today, look at what grew around it. Tradition says Guru Ram Das didn't only dig a pool. He invited traders and craftspeople to come and settle, open shops and build a bazaar beside it. So the town tradition calls Ramdaspur, after him, had three things in one place: a pool to wash in, a market to work in, and a sangat to sing with. That's an idea, not just a town plan. Look back over these days. The Gursikh's morning: rise, bathe, remember. After the morning: work, sitting and standing, with the Name. Blessing others: help someone else remember. The city is that same salok, built in brick. The bath is the pool. The work is the bazaar. The others are the sangat. Holiness isn't kept in a separate place you visit now and then; it's laid out next to the shop. His son, Guru Arjan, later praised the town in a salok, paraphrased: I have seen every place, and none is like you. The Creator himself founded you. Ramdaspur is thick with people, beyond compare. Notice what he praises: not empty silence, but a crowded town, full of buying and selling, with the Name sung in the middle of it. Not that the market is perfect. That the market is not outside the reach of the Name.
screen: `A POOL, A BAZAAR, A SANGAT.` · `THE WEEK'S SALOK, BUILT IN BRICK.` · `NONE IS LIKE YOU, RAMDASPUR.` · `THE MARKET IS NOT OUTSIDE IT.` · then, large: `THE CITY HE BUILT.`

segments.voice: Walk in your mind through the store or street where you'll next shop, the lights, the noise, the line at the counter, a little slower than usual, feeling your feet and noticing the faces of the people working there. At the counter, let one breath be a remembering, with Waheguru if you pray.
The city he built. Tradition says Guru Ram Das gathered a pool, a bazaar and a sangat in one town, Ramdaspur, now Amritsar. Today's word.
Your line: holy in the market. The person across the counter is part of the city too. That's the week.
